Found it — read through the `langgraph` v3 streaming source (this is a beta/experimental API, not documented publicly yet, so I traced it directly). The bug is structural, not a typo.

`message.reasoning` and `message.text` are separate lazy "projections" on the same `ChatModelStream`, but they share one underlying pump: pulling from *either* projection drives the entire graph event stream forward, event by event, and keeps pulling until **that projection's `done` flag is set**. The catch is that `done` only becomes `True` at the message's overall finish event — not when that particular content type (reasoning vs. text) stops producing deltas.

So your first loop, `for delta in message.reasoning:`, doesn't stop when the model transitions from thinking into its answer. It keeps calling the pump — pulling and buffering every subsequent event, including every text-delta event for the actual answer — because from its point of view it's still waiting to see if more reasoning deltas or the finish event show up. The reasoning tokens get printed live as they arrive (correct), but every text-delta event that streams past during that same pumping gets silently absorbed into `message.text`'s internal buffer instead of surfacing to you. The loop only returns once the *whole message* — thinking and answer both — has finished generating.

By the time you reach `for delta in message.text:`, the model is already done. That loop isn't broken — it's just replaying an already-fully-populated buffer, instantly, which is why the answer appears to "not stream": it's actually being dumped all at once right after `</THINKING>` closes, rather than trickling in token by token as it's generated.

The fix has to consume both content types from a single pass over the message's actual arrival order, rather than draining `.reasoning` to exhaustion before ever touching `.text` — because exhausting one projection inherently exhausts the whole underlying message. `ChatModelStream` does expose the raw event stream for exactly this (`for event in message: ...`, yielding the underlying `content-block-delta` events with a `type` of `text-delta` or `reasoning-delta`), which would let you branch per-event and print each piece the moment it arrives, in true chronological order, instead of two sequential full-drain loops.

Want me to rewrite that section of the loop to do that?
Propose a loop, explaining what's exactly inside `stream`

Here's what's actually inside `stream`, then the loop.

**What `stream` is.** `agent.stream_events(..., version="v3")` returns a `GraphRunStream`. It's not a stream of raw data — it's a caller-driven pump wrapper: nothing happens on the graph until *you* iterate one of its projections, and each iteration step pulls exactly one event out of the graph and fans it into whichever projection wants it. It exposes a few native projections as attributes, `.messages` being the one you're using.

**What `stream.messages` is.** A `StreamChannel[ChatModelStream]` — a single-consumer queue. Every time the graph starts a new LLM call (a `message-start` event), the transformer immediately constructs a fresh `ChatModelStream` handle and pushes it onto this channel — *before* any content has arrived, not after the call finishes. So `for message in stream.messages:` hands you a live, still-filling handle for each LLM call as it begins. In your agent, that means one `ChatModelStream` per model turn — if the agent calls a tool, you may get a second one for the follow-up turn after the tool result comes back.

**What each `message` (a `ChatModelStream`) is.** A dispatcher that content-block events get fed into as they're pumped. It exposes `.text` and `.reasoning` as separate lazy views over the same underlying feed — which is exactly the trap: draining either one to exhaustion pumps the *entire* message through, because each one's "done" is the message's overall finish, not "no more of my content type is coming." It also exposes raw iteration — `for event in message:` — which yields the protocol events themselves, one at a time, in true arrival order, and stops correctly at that message's own `message-finish`. That's the one that doesn't have the draining problem, because you're consuming a single feed instead of two separate views fighting over it.

Each event is a dict with `event["event"]` telling you what kind it is. The one you care about is `"content-block-delta"`, whose `event["delta"]` is either `{"type": "text-delta", "text": "..."}` or `{"type": "reasoning-delta", "reasoning": "..."}` — this `type` field is the only thing distinguishing thinking tokens from answer tokens as they arrive.

Here's the loop:

Here's each labeled chunk, then the design question.

**Chunk 1 (lines 85–90) — the filter gate.** This is the "is this event worth looking at" check. `for event in message:` yields every raw protocol event for the message — `message-start`, `content-block-start`, `content-block-delta`, `content-block-finish`, `message-finish`, possibly `error`. Only `content-block-delta` events carry actual streamed content, and only when their `delta` field is a dict (as opposed to `None` or some other shape you don't want to touch) is there anything to print. Everything else gets skipped via `continue`. This chunk's job is purely to narrow the firehose down to "a token just arrived" before either of the content branches has to think about it.

**Chunk 2 (lines 91–96) — the reasoning branch.** Fires only when the delta is a `reasoning-delta` *and* `DISPLAY_THINKING` is on — you folded the `if not DISPLAY_THINKING: continue` I had into the condition itself, which is a fine simplification since there's nothing else that branch needs to do when thinking display is off. On the first reasoning token of this message it opens `<THINKING>` and flips `thinking_gate` so it doesn't reopen the tag on every subsequent token; every reasoning token after that just prints.

**Chunk 3 (lines 97–102) — the text branch.** Fires on `text-delta`. Before printing the actual answer token, it checks whether a thinking block is currently open (`thinking_gate`) and, if so, closes it right there — this is the moment the model has stopped reasoning and started answering, so the tag has to close exactly at that boundary for the output to read correctly. Then it prints the text token itself, whether or not any thinking preceded it.

**Chunk 4 (lines 103–105) — the post-loop cleanup.** Runs once `for event in message:` has exhausted — i.e. this message hit `message-finish`. If `thinking_gate` is still `True` at that point, it means a `<THINKING>` tag got opened but chunk 3 never ran to close it.

**Why you need both closers, not one.** They're triggered by two different signals and cover two situations that can't collapse into a single check:

Chunk 3 closes the tag *in response to an event* — specifically, the arrival of the first `text-delta`. That's the only place in the loop that knows "reasoning just ended, answer just began," and it has to fire at that exact point so `</THINKING>` prints before the answer starts streaming, not after. If you deleted chunk 3 and relied only on chunk 4, the tag would stay open through the entire answer — because chunk 4 only runs after the whole message (including all the text) has finished streaming — so you'd get all the answer text printed first, glued to the still-open thinking block, with `</THINKING>` tacked on at the very end instead of where it actually belongs.

Chunk 4 closes the tag *in response to the loop ending* with no such event ever having arrived. That happens whenever a message reasons but never produces a `text-delta` at all before finishing — the clearest case is a tool-calling turn: the model reasons about which tool to call, emits a `tool_call` block, and hits `message-finish` with zero text blocks. Chunk 3 never fires in that case because its trigger condition (`text-delta`) never occurs, so without chunk 4 you'd be left with a permanently unclosed `<THINKING>` tag in your output for every tool-invoking turn.

So the split isn't redundancy — it's two distinct completions of the same state machine: "reasoning ended because the answer started" vs. "reasoning ended because the message ended without an answer." Neither condition implies the other, so neither closer can substitute for the other.
So this only applies for tool calling. in its current state, chunk 4 is redundant as there will always be a text stream

Not quite — the two claims are different. "Only applies to tool calling" is right as the primary trigger, but "redundant because there will always be a text stream" assumes something the framework doesn't actually guarantee: that's a property of *this specific model's* behavior, not of `create_agent`/`ChatModelStream`/the v3 protocol. Nothing in the code you read requires a `text-delta` to follow a `reasoning-delta` before `message-finish`.

Whether that gap ever fires depends entirely on how your model behaves when it decides to call a tool. Plenty of reasoning-tuned tool-calling models (this is common with Qwen3-style and DeepSeek-R1-style tool use) go straight from `</think>` into the tool-call block with zero filler text — no "Let me check that for you," just reasoning followed immediately by a `tool_call` and `message-finish`. If your current model happens to always emit some commentary before invoking a tool, you won't have observed the gap in testing — but that's "hasn't happened yet," not "can't happen." Swap `MODEL` in `.env`, or the same model under a different system prompt that nudges it toward terser tool use, and the assumption breaks silently — no exception, just a `<THINKING>` tag that never closes and bleeds into whatever prints next.

There's also a second case beyond tool calling: a message that hits `message-finish` mid-thought — context/length limit reached while still reasoning, or an interrupted generation — same shape, same missing closer.

If you want to check empirically rather than take my word for it, ask something that clearly forces a tool call and watch whether any text ever prints before the tool result comes back. If it never does for your model, chunk 4 is still cheap insurance, not dead weight — five lines against a failure mode that's silent and easy to miss in a TUI. I'd keep it.
Ok. Is this normally where we're supposed ti be using LangGraph? To represent this pipeline with graph traversal?

You're already using LangGraph — you just haven't been authoring the graph by hand. `create_agent` isn't an alternative to LangGraph; it's a factory that builds a `StateGraph` for you (a fixed topology: model node → conditional edge → tool node → back to model node, looping until the model stops calling tools) and compiles it. What you get back, `agent`, is literally a `CompiledStateGraph`. `agent.stream_events(...)` — the whole `GraphRunStream`/`Pregel`/mux machinery you've been reading source for — is LangGraph's runtime engine executing that graph, one step at a time. So the pipeline is already graph traversal; `create_agent` just wrote the graph for you because your topology is the extremely common "single agent, call tools, repeat" shape.

You'd reach for the raw `StateGraph` API — defining nodes and edges yourself — when your control flow stops being that shape: multiple specialized agents with a router deciding which one handles a request, a fixed multi-stage pipeline (retrieve → draft → critique → revise) where the steps aren't "keep looping until no more tool calls," parallel branches that fan out and merge, or interrupt points at specific stages for human review rather than just at tool-confirmation boundaries. None of that describes your TUI — one model, one tool loop, one thread. For this shape, `create_agent` is the idiomatic entry point, not a shortcut you've outgrown.

Yes — `CompiledStateGraph` (what `create_agent` returns) has a `.get_graph()` method that returns a drawable `Graph` object, with a few output formats:

`agent.get_graph().print_ascii()` renders it as ASCII art straight to the terminal — no extra dependencies, and it's the one that actually fits a TUI, since everything else needs either a network call or extra packages.

`agent.get_graph().draw_mermaid()` returns a Mermaid syntax string you can paste into a Mermaid live editor or render elsewhere — also zero extra deps, but it's just text output, not a picture.

`agent.get_graph().draw_mermaid_png(output_file_path="graph.png")` and `.draw_png(...)` produce an actual image file, but `draw_mermaid_png` needs either network access to mermaid.ink or a local Playwright install, and `draw_png` needs `pygraphviz`.

For your case — a terminal app, checking this once during dev — `agent.get_graph().print_ascii()` right after you build `agent` (line 54) is the one I'd reach for first; drop it in temporarily, run the script once to see the topology, then remove it. Want me to add it?

Good instinct to question that — the edge is real, the picture is just wrong. I checked both sides:

**The edge exists.** In `create_agent`'s graph-building code (`langchain/agents/factory.py`), the "tools" node gets a conditional edge back to "model": `graph.add_conditional_edges("tools", ..., tools_to_model_destinations)`, where `tools_to_model_destinations` defaults to just `["model"]` — it only adds a route straight to `__end__` if one of your tools was declared with `return_direct=True`, or you're using structured output. Since neither applies here, the routing function attached to "tools" always sends control back to "model" once a tool finishes.

**The renderer just doesn't draw it.** `graph_ascii.py` says right in its own docstring: "Draws DAG in ASCII" — it's built on `grandalf`'s Sugiyama layered-layout algorithm, which fundamentally assumes a directed *acyclic* graph, laid out top to bottom. A `tools → model` edge is a cycle — model sits above tools in the layout, so that edge points backward through layers the algorithm never expected. This particular ASCII renderer (ported from `dvc`'s dagascii tool) doesn't route or draw back-edges at all; it just silently omits them rather than erroring. That's why your printout shows a clean tree — start → model → {tools, end} — with nothing closing the loop.

If you want to actually *see* the cycle, swap the renderer: `print(agent.get_graph().draw_mermaid())` produces Mermaid syntax, and Mermaid handles cycles correctly — LangGraph's own docs use Mermaid specifically for this reason. Paste the output into a Mermaid live editor and you'll see the tools→model arrow completing the loop.

As for the mechanism itself: nothing in the tool node's code "sends a pointer" anywhere. LangGraph's runtime (Pregel — the same actor-style, superstep-based execution model as Google's graph-processing system) decides routing purely from the edges, after each node finishes. When "tools" completes, the engine calls the conditional-edge function attached to that node with the current state, gets back a destination name, and activates whatever node is named — in your case, always `"model"`. The tool function itself has zero awareness of the graph; it just returns a result, and the graph engine — not the node — is what decides "next: model."

There it is — `tools -.-> model` closing the loop, exactly as the factory code predicted. Notice all three routing edges (`model -.-> __end__`, `model -.-> tools`, `tools -.-> model`) use the dashed `-.->` style while `__start__ --> model` is solid — that's Mermaid's convention for conditional vs. unconditional edges, matching the `*` vs `.` distinction you saw in the ASCII version. Same graph, just a renderer that doesn't choke on the cycle.

The clearest gap: tool-call visibility. Your agent already has a working tool (`calculator`, wired through `tools_registrar.py`), the graph already loops correctly through it, but nothing in your streaming loop prints anything when a tool actually gets invoked — right now if the model calls `calculator`, the user sees thinking (maybe), then silence, then the final answer, with no indication a tool ran at all. That gap is even marked in your own code: `util.py` already has a `tool_print` stub and `main.py` imports it, but the call is commented out (line 104) — and as written it wouldn't work anyway, since it expects a `result["messages"]` dict (a finished state snapshot) while `stream` is the live `GraphRunStream` you already drained.

I'd extend the same per-event loop you just fixed for text/reasoning to also watch for tool-call content blocks, so `[TOOL] calculator(...)` (and its result) prints live, right as it happens, instead of bolting on a separate post-hoc scan of the final message list. The tradeoff is that tool-call events have a slightly different shape than the reasoning/text deltas you've already handled (chunked args that build up incrementally, then a finished `tool_call` block), so it's a bit more surface than the two-branch pattern you have now — but it reuses the exact mechanism you already understand rather than introducing a second, different way of inspecting the conversation.

Root cause: `.messages` is scoped to LLM output only, and the tool's return value isn't LLM output. I found the exact filter in `MessagesTransformer._route_protocol_event`:

```python
if event.get("role") == "tool":
    self._ignored_runs.add(run_id)
    return
```

with the comment right above it: *"Tool results are exposed on the tools projection and state snapshots; `run.messages` is the chat-token projection."* Everything you're seeing — `tool_call_chunk` start, the `block-delta` building up `args`, the finished `tool_call` — is the **model** deciding to call `calculator` and streaming out the call it wants to make. That's still LLM-generated content, so it flows through `.messages` like any other token. But the tool actually *running* — your `calculator` function executing and returning `51499` — happens in the graph's "tools" node, which isn't an LLM call at all. Its output gets wrapped in a `ToolMessage` and appended to the graph's state, and the code above deliberately excludes anything tagged `role: "tool"` from the chat-token projection you're iterating.

Where it actually lives: `stream.values` (or `stream.output`, its blocking convenience) — the state-snapshot projection, which is auto-registered alongside `.messages` on every `stream_events(version="v3")` call. It yields the full graph state dict after each step, and once the tools node runs, that state's `"messages"` list has the `ToolMessage` in it, `.content` being the actual return value.

And this lines up exactly with what `tool_print` in `util.py` already expects — `result["messages"]` — it just was never called against the right shape. Once your `for message in stream.messages:` loop finishes, the graph has already run to completion (draining `.messages` pumps the whole run), so `stream.output` is a free, already-computed final state dict at that point. The fix for line 104 is just:

```python
tool_print(stream.output)
```

not `tool_print(stream)` — `stream` itself has no `["messages"]`; `stream.output` does.

# Short-term vs. Long-term Memory in LangGraph

## Conceptual Distinction

**Short-term memory** operates within a single conversation thread, maintaining context for ongoing interactions. **Long-term memory** persists across different sessions and threads, enabling information recall anywhere in the application.

## Storage & API Surfaces

**Short-term Memory:**
- Stored via thread-scoped checkpoints managed by LangGraph
- Implemented as part of the agent's state
- Accessed through the graph's standard state mechanism
- As described: "State is persisted to a database using a checkpointer so the thread can be resumed at any time"

**Long-term Memory:**
- Stored in custom namespaces using LangGraph's `Store` API (BaseStore)
- Organized hierarchically with user/org IDs or application labels
- Supports both semantic search and content filtering
- Retrieved via the store's `get()`, `search()`, and `put()` methods with namespace and key parameters

## Key Differences in Purpose

Short-term memory handles immediate conversational context, including message history and session-specific artifacts. Long-term memory preserves user-specific facts, experiences, and behavioral patterns that inform personalization across multiple separate conversations, addressing what the documentation calls the "complex challenge" of retaining information beyond individual interactions.

# langgraph-checkpoint-sqlite on PyPI

**Existence & Version:** Yes, this package exists on PyPI. The latest version is **3.1.1**, released July 30, 2026.

**Exported Classes:** The package exports two main classes:
- `SqliteSaver` - synchronous checkpoint saver
- `AsyncSqliteSaver` - asynchronous checkpoint saver (via `aiosqlite`)

**Description:** This library provides a SQLite implementation of LangGraph's checkpoint saver, designed for "local development, testing, or lightweight deployments."

**Usage Example (Synchronous):**
```python
from langgraph.checkpoint.sqlite import SqliteSaver

with SqliteSaver.from_conn_string(":memory:") as checkpointer:
    checkpointer.put(write_config, checkpoint, {}, {})
    checkpointer.get(read_config)
    list(checkpointer.list(read_config))
```

**Usage Example (Asynchronous):**
```python
from langgraph.checkpoint.sqlite.aio import AsyncSqliteSaver

async with AsyncSqliteSaver.from_conn_string(":memory:") as checkpointer:
    await checkpointer.aput(write_config, checkpoint, {}, {})
    await checkpointer.aget(read_config)
    [c async for c in checkpointer.alist(read_config)]
```

For step 1, the relevant API is the **checkpointer** — same interface your `InMemorySaver()` already implements, so this is a swap, not a redesign.

**The class to reach for:** `SqliteSaver` (and its async twin `AsyncSqliteSaver`) from `langgraph.checkpoint.sqlite` / `langgraph.checkpoint.sqlite.aio`, package `langgraph-checkpoint-sqlite`. It's file-backed, no server process, explicitly built for "local development... or lightweight deployments" — exactly your case, a single-user local TUI. (Postgres/Mongo/Redis checkpointers exist too, each with async variants under `langgraph.checkpoint.{postgres,mongodb,redis}`, but those are for multi-user server deployments — overkill here.)

**The pattern that's different from `InMemorySaver()`:** database checkpointers are constructed via `.from_conn_string(...)` as a context manager, and need a one-time `checkpointer.setup()` call to create the schema — this is the DB-backed analog of "create the agent once, not per run" that you already internalized earlier: `setup()` runs once ever (or once per fresh DB file), not on every script launch. Point `from_conn_string` at a real file path, not `:memory:` — `:memory:` would give you the exact same "gone on process exit" behavior you have now, just with extra steps.

**The piece the checkpointer doesn't solve for you:** it persists *what happened within a thread_id*, but nothing tracks *which thread_id to resume* across restarts. Right now `agent_thread_config`'s `thread_id` is a fresh `uuid7()` every time the script starts (line 58) — swapping the checkpointer alone would durably save each run's conversation, but every launch would still start a brand-new, disconnected thread, because nothing remembers the old ID. That bookkeeping is on you: something as simple as writing the last-used `thread_id` to a small file next to the sqlite DB and reading it back on startup gets you "resume where I left off"; a proper "pick a session" UX would mean tracking multiple thread IDs yourself (the checkpointer has no built-in "list all threads" call — its `list()` is scoped to one thread's checkpoint history, not a directory of sessions).

Two more calls worth knowing while you build this: `agent.get_state(config)` to inspect what's actually stored for a thread (useful for debugging that persistence is working), and `checkpointer.delete_thread(thread_id)` as the complement — your "start fresh" path once you add one.

What would I gane from instead using the AsyncSqliteSaver class?

Mainly non-blocking I/O — `AsyncSqliteSaver` uses `aiosqlite` under the hood, a genuinely different (non-blocking) driver from the plain `sqlite3` that `SqliteSaver` uses, so checkpoint reads/writes wouldn't stall your event loop while they happen.

The catch: that benefit only matters if something else is running concurrently that could use the freed-up time — a server handling multiple users' turns at once, or a background task (like the title-generation call from the session-picker plan) running while the main conversation is still streaming. Your current loop has neither; it's single-threaded, blocking on `input()`, one turn at a time, nothing else competing for the CPU while a checkpoint write happens. There'd be no measurable win, and the cost is real: you'd have to convert the whole file to async — `agent.astream_events(...)` instead of `.stream_events(...)`, `async for` over `stream.messages`, wrapping `input()` in something that doesn't block the event loop, and `async with AsyncSqliteSaver.from_conn_string(...)` instead of a plain `with`. That's a structural rewrite of the loop for a benefit with nothing to apply it to right now.

I'd stay on the sync `SqliteSaver` — it matches the rest of the codebase as it stands. Worth revisiting only if this ever grows into something with real concurrency (a server backend, multiple simultaneous sessions, background work happening alongside the main turn).

Found the core issue, and it explains your "how do I load it back in" confusion — you can't, because that's not the right mental model here. Let me walk through what's actually wrong.

**The agent still isn't using `memory`.** Line 64 compiles the agent with `checkpointer=InMemorySaver()`, not `memory` (your `SqliteSaver`). So right now, none of the sqlite plumbing you built is actually connected to the running conversation — every turn still checkpoints in-memory only, and `memory.put(...)` at line 94 is writing to a completely separate store the agent never reads from. This is the fix that has to happen before anything else here can work: `checkpointer=memory` on line 64.

**Once that's fixed, you don't need a `/save` command at all.** This is the bigger reframe: a checkpointer isn't something you manually tell to save — LangGraph calls `.put()` on it automatically, as a side effect of every `agent.stream_events(...)` (or `.invoke()`) call. The moment you fix line 64, every single turn is already being durably written to `checkpoints.sqlite` with zero extra code. Your `/save` is trying to reimplement something that's already happening for free, and it's reimplementing it incorrectly — `BaseCheckpointSaver.put()`'s actual signature is `put(config, checkpoint, metadata, new_versions)`, where `checkpoint` is a `Checkpoint` TypedDict (internal fields: `v`, `id`, `ts`, `channel_values`, `channel_versions`, `versions_seen`) — a serialized state snapshot that Pregel constructs during graph execution. Your call passes `checkpoint=agent.checkpointer` — the *checkpointer object itself* — where that snapshot dict is expected. That's the checkpointer/checkpoint mixup baked into the name confusion: the checkpointer is the storage manager; a checkpoint is one saved snapshot it manages. Application code isn't meant to hand-build one.

**Which answers your actual question: there's no "load it into the checkpointer" step, because it's already there.** Once every turn auto-saves, "resuming a session" is entirely about which `thread_id` you point the *config* at for your next call — not about moving data from the store into the checkpointer. Concretely: set `agent_thread_config["configurable"]["thread_id"]` to the thread you want to continue, and the next `agent.stream_events(...)` transparently reads that thread's latest state out of the same sqlite file. `get_tuple()` (what you're calling in `/load`) is for *inspecting* a checkpoint — debugging, time-travel — not for reinstalling one; and right now its result at line 101 isn't even being captured or used.

**The `/list` and `/load` cases have bugs on top of that misconception:**
- `memory.list()` — `list()`'s first parameter, `config`, is required (no default). Calling it with zero arguments throws `TypeError`. Pass `None` to list across every thread, or `agent_thread_config` to scope to just the current one.
- `.list()` returns `Iterator[CheckpointTuple]` — a generator, not a list. `memory.list()[_selected_checkpoint]` will raise `TypeError: 'generator' object is not subscriptable`. You'd need `checkpoints = list(memory.list(None))` first to index into it.
- Each yielded item is a `CheckpointTuple` (`.config`, `.checkpoint`, `.metadata`, ...), not a bare thread_id string — so `{"configurable": {"thread_id": memory.list()[_selected_checkpoint]}}` is putting a whole tuple object where a string is expected. The thread_id is at `checkpoint_tuple.config["configurable"]["thread_id"]`.

One more thing worth flagging: raw checkpoint listing isn't actually the right tool for the session-picker feature you described a couple messages back. A checkpointer auto-saves on *every turn*, so `.list(None)` returns one entry per turn per thread, not one-per-session — and it has no title field at all. That's exactly what the separate `sessions` table (thread_id + title) we discussed is for; `.list()`/`.get_tuple()` are lower-level, for inspecting or time-traveling within one thread's history, not for building the browsable session list.

Want me to fix line 64 now, and then rework `/save`/`/load` into something that actually matches this model — drop `/save` entirely, and make `/load` just switch `thread_id` (backed by the sessions table once that's in place)?
Alright, it's functional. Tell me what exactly a checkpoint is. Is it the entire conversation to that point? So each entry is all of the conversation + the newest entry?

Your intuition is right, with one refinement on granularity.

A checkpoint is a full snapshot of every **channel's** current value at one point in the graph's execution — not a diff, not just the newest turn. "Channel" is the underlying concept: your graph's state schema (the thing with the `messages` key) is modeled as a set of channels, and `messages` specifically uses a reducer (`add_messages`) that merges new entries into a growing list. The checkpoint's `channel_values["messages"]` field holds that list's *current full value* at the time of the snapshot — so yes, each checkpoint effectively contains the entire conversation up to that point, not merely "the conversation so far plus this one new delta." If you fetched checkpoint #12 in a thread's history, you'd get the whole message list as it stood after step 12, ready to use standalone.

The refinement: it's not one checkpoint per user message — it's one checkpoint per graph **step** (what LangGraph calls a superstep, roughly "one node finished running"). Your agent's loop is `model → tools → model`, and each of those transitions produces its own checkpoint. So a single conversational turn that involves a tool call generates *three* checkpoints, not one — this is why `.list(None)` will return far more entries than "one per thing you typed," and it's the concrete reason raw checkpoint listing is the wrong granularity for the session picker: it's step-level, your sessions table needs to be conversation-level.

The other fields on `Checkpoint` exist to support that step-by-step nature: `id` is monotonically increasing so checkpoints within a thread form an orderable chain (this is what "time-travel debugging" in the docs refers to — you can rewind to any prior checkpoint, not just the latest), and `channel_versions`/`versions_seen` are how the graph engine itself decides what to run next — a node becomes eligible to execute when it's seen a newer version of its input channel than what it last processed, which is the actual mechanism behind the conditional-edge routing we looked at earlier (tools → model isn't "the tool sends a signal," it's "the model channel just got a version bump the model node hasn't seen yet, so it's eligible to run").
So, without time travel implemened, I technically only need to store the freshest checkpoint, because I wont be rolling back. So each conversation will have only one checkpoint, true?

Not quite — that's true of what you *read*, but not of what actually gets *written*.

Looking at `SqliteSaver`'s actual table schema:

```sql
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS checkpoints (
    thread_id TEXT NOT NULL,
    checkpoint_ns TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT '',
    checkpoint_id TEXT NOT NULL,
    ...
    PRIMARY KEY (thread_id, checkpoint_ns, checkpoint_id)
);
```

The primary key includes `checkpoint_id`, not just `thread_id`. Since every checkpoint gets its own unique, monotonically-increasing ID (from the `Checkpoint.id` field we looked at), every single `.put()` call *inserts a new row* — it never overwrites the row for that thread. And `.put()` fires once per graph step (once after `model`, once after `tools`, once after the follow-up `model`), not once per conversation, unconditionally, as part of normal graph execution — this happens whether or not you ever plan to use time travel. Not implementing rollback in your app doesn't stop the graph from writing every step; it just means you never *read* the older rows back.

What actually matches your intuition is `get_tuple()`'s read path: when you resume with just a `thread_id` and no explicit `checkpoint_id`, it runs `ORDER BY checkpoint_id DESC LIMIT 1` — grabs the newest row and nothing else. So functionally, resuming a conversation only ever touches the latest checkpoint per thread, exactly as you'd expect. But storage-wise, every step of every turn is still sitting in the file, accumulating indefinitely — a long conversation with several tool-calling turns could easily leave a few dozen rows behind under one `thread_id`, all but the last one permanently unread by anything.

If that growth bothers you, that's a separate thing you'd manage explicitly (there's no "only keep latest" flag on the checkpointer) — either periodically pruning older rows for threads you don't need history for, or just not worrying about it, since sqlite handles a few thousand small rows per thread without issue for a single-user local tool. Not something you need to solve now, just worth knowing it's happening.

`memory.list(None)` already gives you this for free — `None` for `config` means "no thread filter, list across every thread," and its SQL query is unconditionally `ORDER BY checkpoint_id DESC` — newest first, globally, not just within one thread. Since checkpoint IDs are monotonically increasing, the very first item that generator yields is the most recently written checkpoint in the whole database, whichever thread it belongs to.

```python
latest = next(memory.list(None), None)
if latest is not None:
    agent_thread_config["configurable"]["thread_id"] = latest.config["configurable"]["thread_id"]
```

`next(..., None)` matters here — `.list()` is a generator, so this pulls exactly one row off the top rather than materializing every checkpoint in the file just to throw away all but the first; and the `None` default handles the empty-database case (first run ever, nothing to resume) by just keeping the freshly generated `uuid7()` you already have on line 66.

This slots in right after `agent_thread_config` is built (line 68), before the REPL starts, if you want "always resume the latest conversation on launch." If you'd rather this be an explicit action instead of automatic, the same two lines are what your `/load` case should be doing under the hood — same lookup, just triggered by the command instead of at startup.

Reuse the same `sqlite_connection` you already have open — no need for a second connection to the same file. A `sessions` table alongside `memory`'s own `checkpoints`/`writes` tables, created once at startup right after `memory.setup()`:

```python
sqlite_connection.execute("""
    CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS sessions (
        thread_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
        title TEXT,
        created_at TEXT DEFAULT (datetime('now')),
        updated_at TEXT DEFAULT (datetime('now'))
    )
""")
sqlite_connection.commit()
```

Then a small upsert helper — `ON CONFLICT` because a thread might get (re)named more than once, not just created once:

```python
def set_session_title(conn, thread_id, title):
    conn.execute(
        """
        INSERT INTO sessions (thread_id, title, updated_at)
        VALUES (?, ?, datetime('now'))
        ON CONFLICT(thread_id) DO UPDATE SET title = excluded.title, updated_at = excluded.updated_at
        """,
        (thread_id, title),
    )
    conn.commit()
```

For the actual naming trigger, I'd start with the simplest possible path rather than jumping straight to the LLM-generated title from a few messages back: a manual `/name <title>` command that calls `set_session_title(sqlite_connection, agent_thread_config["configurable"]["thread_id"], title)`. That gives you an end-to-end write path you can verify works — table exists, upsert works, reading it back for the picker works — before layering the "self-assigned" auto-title (a separate `model.invoke(...)` call after the first turn) on top of infrastructure you've already confirmed is solid. Same "infrastructure first" order you set at the start of this whole thread.

Want me to wire the table creation and `/name` command into the file now?

Good structure overall — the table setup and the `set_session_title` design match what we discussed. Two bugs would stop `/name` from working at all, plus the older `/load`/`/list` issues are still sitting there untouched.

**Blocking bug — column name typo in `util.py`:**

```python
sqlite_connection.execute("""
    INSERT INTO sessions (threads_id, title, updated_at)
    ...
```

The table was created with `thread_id` (singular "thread"), but the `INSERT` column list says `threads_id` (plural). The `ON CONFLICT(thread_id) ...` clause right below it uses the correct spelling — so the two don't even agree with each other, let alone with the actual schema. This will raise `sqlite3.OperationalError: table sessions has no column named threads_id` the instant `/name` is used.

**Bigger bug — the slash commands fall through into a chat turn.** Only `case "help":` has a `continue`. `name`, `list`, and `load` all fall through past the `match` block into `messages.append(HumanMessage(user_input))` and the full `agent.stream_events(...)` call — meaning after typing `/name`, entering a title, and successfully saving it, the code then sends the literal string `"/name"` to the model as if it were a real chat message, and the model will try to respond to it. Same thing happens for `/list` and `/load`. Each of those cases needs its own `continue` right after it finishes.

**`/list` won't show anything readable.** `memory.list(None)` returns a generator; `print(memory.list(None))` prints something like `<generator object ... at 0x...>`, not the checkpoints themselves. You'd want to materialize and iterate it — e.g. `for cp in memory.list(None): print(cp.config["configurable"]["thread_id"], cp.metadata)` — to see anything useful.

**`/load` is unchanged from before** and still has the three bugs I flagged last time: `memory.list()` is called with zero arguments even though `config` is required (`TypeError`), the result is indexed (`[...]`) even though `.list()` returns a generator, not a list, and even past that, `memory.list()[_selected_checkpoint]` is a whole `CheckpointTuple` object being passed where a bare `thread_id` string belongs. Looks like this one just hasn't been touched yet rather than being a new issue.

One unrelated pre-existing thing worth knowing about while you're in here: `user_input.strip()[0] == '/'` will raise `IndexError` on an empty input (just pressing Enter) — `""[0]` is out of range, and that exception isn't caught by the `except KeyboardInterrupt` you have, so it'll crash the whole loop. Not part of what you just wrote, just flagging it since you're touching this exact line.

Want me to fix the typo, add the missing `continue`s, and clean up `/list`'s output?
How can i query the sessions table only for listing

A plain `SELECT` against the table directly — no need to touch `memory`/`SqliteSaver` at all, this table is entirely yours, outside LangGraph's API surface:

```python
def list_sessions(sqlite_connection):
    return sqlite_connection.execute(
        "SELECT thread_id, title, updated_at FROM sessions ORDER BY updated_at DESC"
    ).fetchall()
```

`updated_at` sorts correctly as a plain string here since `datetime('now')` produces a fixed-width `YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS` format — lexicographic order matches chronological order, so `ORDER BY updated_at DESC` gives you most-recently-active session first without needing a real date type.

I'd put that in `util.py` next to `set_session_title`, same pattern. Then `/list` becomes:

```python
case "list":
    for thread_id, title, updated_at in list_sessions(sqlite_connection):
        print(f"{title or '(untitled)'}  [{thread_id}]  updated {updated_at}")
    continue
```

This also resolves the earlier `/list` complaint for free — you're iterating real rows now instead of `print()`-ing a `CheckpointTuple` generator's repr. And this is the piece `/load` should be built on too, once you're ready to fix it: list from `sessions`, let the user pick a row, then just set `agent_thread_config["configurable"]["thread_id"]` to that row's `thread_id` — no `memory.get_tuple(...)` needed, since (as covered earlier) the graph reads the right checkpoint automatically the next time you invoke with that thread_id.

Good instinct catching the disconnect — and the stub in `self_name.py` has a real bug on top of being empty: it references `@tool` but never imports it (`from langchain.tools import tool` is missing), so it'll `NameError` the moment `tools_registrar.py` tries to import it.

Here's the design, addressing both the prompting question and the plumbing problem underneath it:

**The tool itself — description is the actual instruction.** LangChain's `@tool` decorator pulls the tool's `description` straight from its docstring, and that description is the primary signal the model uses to decide *when* to call something — not just what it does. Write it prescriptively:

```python
from langchain.tools import tool

@tool
def self_name(title: str) -> str:
    """Assign a short, descriptive title (3-6 words) to this conversation.
    Call this exactly once, right after you send your very first reply in a
    brand new conversation. Do not call it again unless the user explicitly
    asks to rename the conversation. Do not tell the user you are doing
    this — call it silently, as a background action."""
    return title
```

Note it just returns `title` — it doesn't touch the database itself. That's deliberate, and it's the answer to a problem you'd otherwise hit: `self_name.py` has no natural way to reach `sqlite_connection` or the live `thread_id` without either a circular import back to `main.py` or dragging in dependency-injection machinery (`ToolRuntime`) that's overkill for a single-file prototype. Keeping the tool a pure echo sidesteps that entirely.

**Where the actual write happens — `main.py`, parallel to `print_tool_use`.** That's already scanning `stream.output["messages"]` for `ToolMessage`s after every turn; add a matching pass for this one specifically, right after your `print_tool_use(stream.output)` call:

```python
for r in stream.output["messages"][-4:]:
    if isinstance(r, ToolMessage) and r.name == "self_name":
        set_session_title(sqlite_connection, agent_thread_config["configurable"]["thread_id"], r.content)
        break
```

**Keeping it invisible.** Two separate things make it silent, not one: your streaming loop already only branches on `reasoning-delta`/`text-delta` — nothing renders tool-call events live, so the call itself never appears mid-stream regardless of which tool it is. The part you *do* need to guard is `print_tool_use`, which currently prints `[TOOL] {name}: {content}` for every `ToolMessage` it finds — left as-is, it'll print `[TOOL] self_name: <title>` on every first turn. Give it a one-line exclusion:

```python
def print_tool_use(result) -> None:
    _start = len(result["messages"])-2
    _end = max(0, _start-MAX_TOOL_CALLS+1)
    for r in result["messages"][_start:_end:-1]:
        if isinstance(r, ToolMessage) and r.name != "self_name":
            print(f"[TOOL] {r.name}: {r.content}")
```

**System prompt reinforcement.** The tool description alone is often enough, but for a model that doesn't reliably act on tool descriptions without a nudge, add one line to `SYSTEM_PROMPT` restating the trigger condition — this is exactly what a system prompt is for, background operating instructions the user never sees: *"After your first reply in a new conversation, call `self_name` with a short title. Never mention this to the user."*

Last thing: `tools_registrar.py` still has `TOOLS = [calculator]` — `self_name` is imported but never added to the list, so none of this fires until you fix that too.
Is this tool-based approach meaningful, or is there a smarter way of implementing this mechanic?

Honestly, no — tool-calling is heavier machinery than this task needs. Titling isn't a judgment call worth embedding in the model's own reasoning; it's a deterministic "always do this once, right after turn one" side effect that the *app* already knows the exact trigger for, without needing to ask the model's permission through a tool it now has to carry in its schema on every single turn for the rest of the conversation — and might occasionally just not call, since tool-triggering is probabilistic even with a well-written description. That's also why you needed to filter it out of `print_tool_use` and rely on the streaming loop happening to not render tool events — you're doing extra work to hide the seams of a mechanism that's fighting the task's actual shape.

The plainer alternative — which is closer to what I originally pointed you at, before "self-assigned" pulled this toward tool-calling — is a direct, second `model.invoke([...])` call from `main.py` itself, outside the agent entirely, fired right after the first exchange completes: give it the first user message and reply, ask for a short title, write the result straight to `sessions`. Same model, zero tool-schema overhead on every later turn, no probabilistic "did it actually decide to call it" risk, and nothing to hide from the streaming loop because it was never part of the tool-call stream in the first place.

What you'd give up: the model ever deciding *on its own* to retitle mid-conversation if the topic drifts. If that's something you actually want, tool-calling is the right primitive for it. But for "title it once, automatically, right after the first reply" — I'd drop the tool and just make the direct call.

Found it — and there's a hard blocker before we even get to the new logic: `util.py` has a syntax error that will crash the whole program on startup.

```python
def self_assign_title()

def set_session_title(sqlite_connection, thread_id:str, title:str) -> None:
```

Line 18 — `def self_assign_title()` has no colon and no body. This isn't a runtime bug, it's a parse error: `from util import ...` in `main.py` will fail before a single line of your program executes. Looks like a leftover stub from when you started factoring the naming logic into a helper and then inlined it into `main.py` instead — since the logic already lives there now, I'd just delete this dangling line rather than finish it.

Once that's cleared, the inlined call itself has four separate issues stacked on each other:

```python
if not session_has_name:
    set_session_title(
        sqlite_connection,
        agent_thread_config["configurable"]["thread_id"],
        model.invoke({"messages": HumanMessage("Give a short, descriptive title (3-6 words) to this conversation.")})
    )
```

1. **`{"messages": HumanMessage(...)}` is the wrong shape.** That dict-with-a-`"messages"`-key input is for invoking the *graph* (`agent.stream_events({"messages": messages}, ...)`) — a plain `model.invoke(...)` on your bare `ChatOllama` wants a message list, not that dict. It needs `model.invoke([...])`.

2. **No conversation content is actually passed in.** The call sends only the bare instruction — the model has nothing to summarize, since neither the user's message nor its own reply is included. `stream.output["messages"]` is sitting right there already (you just used it for `print_tool_use`), and it holds the full exchange including the reply that was just generated — that's what should go into the title call.

3. **`model.invoke(...)` returns an `AIMessage`, not a string** — you're passing the whole message object as `title`. `set_session_title` binds it straight into a sqlite parameter, and sqlite can't bind an arbitrary Python object; this will raise `sqlite3.InterfaceError` at runtime. Needs `.content`.

4. **`session_has_name` never gets set to `True`.** It's initialized once before the loop and nothing inside the loop ever flips it — so once the above stops crashing, this fires after *every* turn, not just the first.

Put together:

```python
if not session_has_name:
    title = model.invoke(
        stream.output["messages"]
        + [HumanMessage("Give a short, descriptive title (3-6 words) for this conversation. Respond with only the title.")]
    ).content
    set_session_title(sqlite_connection, agent_thread_config["configurable"]["thread_id"], title)
    session_has_name = True
```

One design note beyond the bugs: tracking "has this been named" as a local boolean is fragile the moment `/load` switches you to a different thread mid-run — the flag doesn't know which thread it's actually describing. Checking the `sessions` table directly (does a row already exist for this `thread_id`?) instead of a separate in-memory flag would stay correct across `/load` for free, since it'd be reading the same source of truth `/list` and `/load` already use.
the messages var carries only the user inputs, while the server side and agent checkpointer has both sides of the conversation in the checkpoints, correct?

Correct on both counts.

`messages` (the local Python list) only ever grows via `messages.append(HumanMessage(user_input))` — nothing in the loop ever appends the assistant's reply, a tool call, or a tool result to it. It's purely a running list of what the user typed, turn after turn.

The checkpointer has the full bidirectional history because of how the merge works: when you call `agent.stream_events({"messages": messages}, config=agent_thread_config, ...)`, that input doesn't *replace* the checkpointed state for that `thread_id` — it gets merged into it via the `messages` channel's reducer (`add_messages`), which appends by message ID rather than overwriting. So even though your local `messages` var has no idea the assistant ever said anything, the graph's own persisted state already has every prior `AIMessage` and `ToolMessage` sitting in it from when they were generated on earlier turns — your new `HumanMessage` just lands on top of that existing history inside the checkpoint, not in place of it. That's exactly the mechanism behind `stream.output["messages"]` having the full exchange available for the title call, while `messages` locally only ever had the human side.

One thing that falls out of this worth noting: since the reducer merges by ID and the checkpointer already retains everything, resending your whole growing local `messages` list every turn (rather than just the newest `HumanMessage`) isn't adding information the checkpoint doesn't already have — the older entries just get matched and no-op'd by ID. Not a bug, just redundant work on every call as the list gets longer.

content.text:
`agent.get_state(agent_thread_config).values["messages"]` — this is the general-purpose way, independent of any particular stream.

`get_state` is doing exactly what you'd expect from everything we've already looked at: internally it just calls `checkpointer.get_tuple(config)` — the same method underlying `/load` — fetches the latest checkpoint for that `thread_id`, and wraps it into a `StateSnapshot`. That snapshot's `.values` field is literally the current channel values dict, `{"messages": [...]}` — same shape as `stream.output`, but not tied to having just run a turn.

That's the practical difference from what you're using now: `stream.output["messages"]` only exists right after `agent.stream_events(...)` has been called and driven to completion — it's scoped to one specific in-flight stream object. `agent.get_state(agent_thread_config)` works for any thread_id at any point, whether or not a message was just sent — so it'd also work if you wanted to, say, preview a session's content right after `/load`ing it, before the user's typed anything new.

For your title-generation call specifically, it's a direct drop-in — `agent.get_state(agent_thread_config).values["messages"]` instead of `stream.output["messages"]` gives you the same list right after a turn completes, but leaves you with a mechanism that keeps working even if you later move that logic somewhere that doesn't have `stream` in scope.

Progress on the structure — `is_session_named` is the right idea (checking the DB instead of a fragile flag), and dropping the standalone `messages` accumulator is correct. But there are three bugs that will crash this on the very first turn of any conversation, in the order they'd actually fire:

**1. `is_session_named` crashes immediately, and even if it didn't, the logic is wrong.**

```python
def is_session_named(sqlite_connection, thread_id:str):
    return len(sqlite_connection.execute("SELECT thread_id FROM sessions")) == 1
```

`sqlite_connection.execute(...)` returns a `Cursor`, not a list — `len()` on a cursor raises `TypeError: object of type 'Cursor' has no len()` outright. Separately, the query has no `WHERE` clause, so it's not even looking at *this* thread — it's counting rows across the entire `sessions` table, and `thread_id` (the parameter) is never used at all. What you actually want:

```python
def is_session_named(sqlite_connection, thread_id: str) -> bool:
    row = sqlite_connection.execute(
        "SELECT 1 FROM sessions WHERE thread_id = ?", (thread_id,)
    ).fetchone()
    return row is not None
```

**2. `_convo_so_far + HumanMessage(...)` — concatenating a list with a bare message.**

```python
_convo_so_far = agent.get_state(agent_thread_config).values["messages"]
...
model.invoke(_convo_so_far+HumanMessage("Give a short, descriptive title..."))
```

`_convo_so_far` is a `list`; `list.__add__` requires the other operand to also be a list. `list + HumanMessage(...)` raises `TypeError: can only concatenate list (not "HumanMessage") to list`. Needs `_convo_so_far + [HumanMessage("...")]`.

**3. Same bug from last time, still unfixed:** `set_session_title(...)`'s third argument is `model.invoke(...)` directly — that returns an `AIMessage`, and it still needs `.content` before it can be bound as a sqlite parameter.

None of these three are caught by `except KeyboardInterrupt`, and `is_session_named` runs unconditionally on every turn — so as it stands, the program will crash on message one of any conversation, before even reaching the concatenation or `.content` bugs.

One piece of cleanup while you're in here: `messages = []` at line 85 is now dead — nothing reads or writes it anymore since the stream call switched to `[HumanMessage(user_input)]` directly at line 116.

Checked the actual conversion code (`langchain_ollama/chat_models.py`, `_convert_messages_to_ollama_messages`) — it's not a crash risk. It's purely structural: for each `AIMessage` in the list, it reads `message.tool_calls` and maps them into the outgoing Ollama request's `tool_calls` field, with zero validation against whatever tools happen to be bound on this particular call:

```python
elif isinstance(message, AIMessage):
    role = "assistant"
    tool_calls = (
        [_lc_tool_call_to_openai_tool_call(tool_call) for tool_call in message.tool_calls]
        if message.tool_calls
        else None
    )
```

So the LangChain/Ollama-client layer will happily serialize a historical tool call into the request even when this specific `.invoke()` has no `tools=` bound at all — nothing here raises or blocks it.

The actual risk is one layer further down, at the model's own chat template — the Jinja template bundled with the GGUF that turns the message list into the literal text prompt. Templates typically render two separate things: the `tools` field (a declaration up front — "here's what's callable this turn") and each assistant message's `tool_calls` (the historical record of what was called). Normally those two only ever appear together, because a model can't call a tool that wasn't declared. Sending tool-call history with an empty `tools` field produces a prompt shape the model was never trained on: it sees its own past self referencing a tool call, with nothing telling it that tool currently exists. Nothing crashes — the request goes through fine — but the model's behavior there is genuinely undefined: at best it just ignores the stray tool-call context and answers the title question normally; at worst it gets pulled toward pattern-matching its own prior tool-call syntax (which would just produce inert, non-functional text, since no `tools` were declared to actually route it anywhere) instead of producing a clean title.

So the concrete thing to watch for isn't an exception — it's a garbled or oddly-formatted title specifically on conversations where `calculator` got used before the auto-naming fired. Worth that test case for exactly this reason.
What fix do you propose?

Strip the tool-call plumbing out before it reaches the toolless call — that's the direct fix for the mismatch, and it's arguably a better title-generation input anyway, since *how* a tool got invoked isn't relevant to what the conversation was about.

A small helper in `util.py`, next to your other session helpers:

```python
def strip_tool_context(messages: list[BaseMessage]) -> list[BaseMessage]:
    cleaned = []
    for m in messages:
        if isinstance(m, ToolMessage):
            continue
        if isinstance(m, AIMessage) and m.tool_calls:
            cleaned.append(AIMessage(content=m.content))
        else:
            cleaned.append(m)
    return cleaned
```

Drops `ToolMessage`s entirely (the tool's raw output isn't conversational content anyway) and, for an `AIMessage` that made a tool call, keeps its text content but discards the `tool_calls` field — so what reaches the title-generation call is just the plain back-and-forth: what the user asked, what the model actually said in reply. An `AIMessage` whose turn was purely a tool invocation (near-empty `.content`) just contributes nothing, harmlessly.

Wire it in where the state gets pulled:

```python
self_naming_prompt = strip_tool_context(agent.get_state(agent_thread_config).values["messages"])
self_naming_prompt.append(HumanMessage("Give a short, descriptive title (3-6 words) to this conversation."))
```

This is a general fix rather than one that leans on "naming only ever fires on turn one" — if you ever change when auto-naming triggers, or the first turn involves several tool calls before the final answer, this still holds up without needing to special-case it. `AIMessage`, `ToolMessage`, and `BaseMessage` are already imported in `main.py`; `util.py` just needs `AIMessage`/`BaseMessage` added to its existing `langchain.messages` import.

Good news first: the core mechanism (`strip_tool_context`, `is_session_named`, `set_session_title`, the naming call) is all internally consistent now, `self_name.py` is already gone (no orphaned dead file), and the `util.py` import split you/the linter made — `BaseMessage` out of `langchain.messages` into `langchain_core.messages.base` — is actually required, not just style: I checked, `langchain.messages` genuinely doesn't export `BaseMessage`, only the concrete subclasses. That would've been an `ImportError` if left as one line.

Four things worth handling before the commit, ordered by how much they'd actually bite you:

**1. `requirements.txt` doesn't pin `langgraph` itself.** It has `langchain`, `langchain-ollama`, `langgraph-checkpoint-sqlite`, `grandalf`, `python-dotenv` — but langgraph is only pulled in transitively through `langchain`. Given the entire streaming loop is built on `stream_events(version="v3")`, which every doc and warning you've seen calls explicitly experimental/beta, a future `pip install -r requirements.txt` could silently resolve a different langgraph version whose internal shape (`ChatModelStream`, `GraphRunStream`, the event schema) has moved out from under this code, with nothing telling you why it broke. Pin it: `langgraph==1.2.11` (what's actually installed and what this was built against).

**2. Dead imports accumulated in `main.py`:** `json`, `tool` (from `langchain.tools`), `SystemMessage`, `AIMessage`, `ToolMessage`, `GraphRunStream`, `StreamChannel`, `InMemorySaver`. None of these are referenced anywhere in the current file — they're leftovers from approaches that got replaced (the old in-memory checkpointer, the abandoned tool-based self-naming attempt, an earlier explicit `GraphRunStream` type annotation). Worth trimming so the import block reflects what the file actually does now.

**3. `tools/calculator.py`'s docstring has a stray quote.** Line 33 starts with `""""` — four quote characters, not three. Python parses it fine (triple-quote opens the string, the fourth is just its first literal character), but it means the tool's actual `.description` — what the model sees on every tool-choice decision — begins with a bare `"` character: `"Evaluate a basic arithmetic expression...`. Cosmetic, but visible in every request.

**4. No fallback case for unrecognized `/` commands.** `match user_input[1:]` has `help`/`name`/`list`/`load` but no `case _:` — typing `/foo` just silently does nothing and falls through to `continue`. Not a crash, just a quiet dead end where a one-line "unknown command, try /help" would help.

One thing that's fine as-is but worth a conscious call: `.env` isn't in `.gitignore` (only `.venv`, `__pycache__`, `*.sqlite` are). There's nothing secret in it right now — just local model hyperparameters, no API keys, since it's all local Ollama — so committing it isn't a security issue today. Just flagging it's a deliberate choice, not an oversight, in case that changes later.

No — three problems, and one of them means it'll fail outright, not just be unsafe.

**It'll actually error as written.** `thread_id` is a string like `"01912e0e-1234-7abc-..."`, and it's f-string-interpolated raw into the query with no quotes: `WHERE thread_id = {thread_id}` becomes literal SQL like `WHERE thread_id = 01912e0e-1234-...`. That's not a valid string literal — SQLite will try to parse the hyphens as subtraction between bare identifiers and throw `sqlite3.OperationalError: near ...: syntax error`. This isn't a "works but is risky" situation, it's just broken.

**Even fixed for that, it's the wrong pattern — and inconsistent with the rest of this file.** Every other function here (`is_session_named`, `set_session_title`, `list_sessions`) uses parameterized `?` placeholders with a params tuple, specifically to avoid building SQL by string interpolation. `thread_id` values in this app currently only ever come from `uuid7()` or from picking an existing row via `/load`, so the injection surface is narrow right now — but it's still the pattern that would bite you the moment anything changes (and notably, this is exactly the shape the original `/load` design had before you switched to numbered selection — worth not reintroducing it here).

**It's also missing `.commit()`.** `set_session_title` right below it calls `sqlite_connection.commit()` after its write; `delete_session` doesn't call it at all, so the deletes may never actually persist to disk depending on the connection's transaction state.

```python
def delete_session(sqlite_connection, thread_id: str) -> None:
    sqlite_connection.execute("DELETE FROM checkpoints WHERE thread_id = ?", (thread_id,))
    sqlite_connection.execute("DELETE FROM writes WHERE thread_id = ?", (thread_id,))
    sqlite_connection.execute("DELETE FROM sessions WHERE thread_id = ?", (thread_id,))
    sqlite_connection.commit()
```

Table order doesn't matter here — no foreign keys were declared across `checkpoints`/`writes`/`sessions`, so there's nothing enforcing deletion order between them.

Found it — the delete never actually happens. Look at what runs when the user confirms:

```python
case "delete":
    sessions = list_sessions(sqlite_connection)
    for i, (thread_id, title, updated_at) in enumerate(sessions, start=1):
        print(f"{i}. {title or '(untitled)'}  updated {updated_at}")
    selected = int(input(" > Enter index of session to delete: ")) - 1
    confirm = input("Confirm session deletion by typing YES: ")
    if confirm == "YES":
        agent_thread_config["configurable"]["thread_id"] = sessions[selected][0]
    else:
        print("Delete not confirmed.\n")
```

On confirmation, this sets `agent_thread_config["configurable"]["thread_id"]` to the selected session — that's the `/load` behavior, not delete. `delete_session(...)` is never called anywhere in this block. It looks like this was copy-pasted from `case "load":` and the confirmation branch never got swapped over to actually call the delete function.

Compounding it: `delete_session` isn't even imported into `main.py`. Line 19 only pulls in `print_tool_use, set_session_title, list_sessions, is_session_named, strip_tool_context` — if you did call `delete_session(...)` right now, you'd get `NameError: name 'delete_session' is not defined`.

The fix:

```python
from util import print_tool_use, set_session_title, list_sessions, is_session_named, strip_tool_context, delete_session
```

```python
if confirm == "YES":
    delete_session(sqlite_connection, sessions[selected][0])
    print("Session deleted.")
else:
    print("Delete not confirmed.\n")
```

One edge case worth being aware of, not necessarily fixing right now: if the user deletes the session they're *currently* in (`sessions[selected][0] == agent_thread_config["configurable"]["thread_id"]`), nothing stops that — you'd keep chatting under a thread_id whose row and checkpoints just got wiped, and the next message would silently start fresh under that same ID (LangGraph treats an unknown `thread_id` as "nothing to resume," not an error), triggering the auto-naming flow again as if it were new. Not a crash, just a UX wrinkle — up to you whether it's worth guarding against.

Small unrelated thing while you're in this block: `/help` still only lists `/name`, `/list`, `/load` — worth adding a line for `/delete` too.

Big problem with placement: this runs on *every* normal exit, not once.

```python
    except KeyboardInterrupt:
        print("\nctrl+c caught. terminating.")
        break

sqlite_connection.execute("""DELETE FROM sessions""")
sqlite_connection.execute("""DELETE FROM writes""")
sqlite_connection.execute("""DELETE FROM checkpoints""")
sqlite_connection.commit()
```

This sits after the `while True:` loop, at module top-level — not inside it, not gated by any flag or confirmation. The only two ways out of that loop are typing `quit` or `Ctrl+C`, and both fall straight through to this block. So as written, this isn't a one-time "start clean" action — it's "wipe every session, every checkpoint, everything, unconditionally, every single time you close the app." Run it once now to clear your test data, and it'll do the exact same thing again the next time you quit after a real conversation, with no warning and no way to opt out. If a real crash (an uncaught exception mid-loop) kills the process instead, it'd actually be *spared* — only the graceful, everyday exit path triggers the wipe, which is backwards from what you'd want.

There's also `wipe_unnamed_sessions` sitting in `util.py`, imported into `main.py` (line 19) but never called anywhere — and it's still an empty stub (`pass`, does nothing). That name suggests what's probably the actually-useful version of this idea: clear out abandoned/never-named sessions specifically, not everything indiscriminately — a much safer "start clean" than nuking named conversations you meant to keep.

For what you actually want right now — wipe everything once, as a deliberate action — I'd pull those four lines out of `main.py` entirely and run them as a one-off, separate from the app:

```
.venv/bin/python -c "
import sqlite3
conn = sqlite3.connect('checkpoints.sqlite')
conn.execute('DELETE FROM sessions')
conn.execute('DELETE FROM writes')
conn.execute('DELETE FROM checkpoints')
conn.commit()
"
```

That way `main.py` goes back to just being the app, with nothing destructive lurking in its normal exit path.

18	def _eval(node):
19	    if isinstance(node, ast.Constant) and isinstance(node.value, (int, float)):
20	        return node.value
21	    if isinstance(node, ast.BinOp) and type(node.op) in _BIN_OPS:
22	        left, right = _eval(node.left), _eval(node.right)
23	        # Guard against resource-exhaustion via huge exponents (e.g. 2**10**9).

26	        return _BIN_OPS[type(node.op)](left, right)
27	    if isinstance(node, ast.UnaryOp) and type(node.op) in _UNARY_OPS:
28	        return _UNARY_OPS[type(node.op)](_eval(node.operand))

The refactor since I last looked is solid too: streaming logic moved into `util.stream_output`, the naming prompt moved out to a file, and `/delete` now supports multi-index deletion.

On next steps: context management is genuinely worth building, but it's a fairly narrow "how do you manage a token budget" exercise. For FDE interview prep specifically, I'd weight higher toward something this project is missing entirely — **a tool that integrates with a real external system** (a REST API, a file/CSV source, a small local DB you don't already own). FDE interviews are less about LLM internals and more about "here's a messy, underspecified integration — go wire it up fast and defend your choices," and right now your only tool is `calculator`, which doesn't exercise that muscle at all.

If you want, I can pitch you a rough spec the way an interviewer would (deliberately a little ambiguous) for a second tool, and you build it against the clock — that practices the actual interview format, not just the code. Otherwise I'm happy to go straight into context management instead; your call.

I have around 10gb PDFs with very good text formatting (for most of them). They are all about a specific domain, that my local model definitely has not been trained on. I would be interested in building a RAG pipeline for them.

Good problem for this — RAG over a large domain-specific corpus is also one of the more common FDE-style builds (ingestion pipeline, retrieval quality tuning, defending design choices under ambiguity). Before I start, two architectural decisions are genuinely yours to make since they shape everything downstream:

questions.question: How should document retrieval plug into the existing agent loop?

options.label: Agentic tool call (Recommended)
options.description: Add a `search_docs` tool the model can decide to invoke, same pattern as calculator. Keeps irrelevant context out of non-domain questions, and is the more realistic 'design a tool for an agent' exercise FDE interviews probe.

options.label: Always-on retrieval
options.description: Every user turn automatically retrieves top-k chunks and injects them into context before the model sees the message. Simpler pipeline, but wastes tokens/pollutes context on turns that aren't about the documents, and you lose the ability to reason about 'did it choose to look this up.'

questions.question: Which local vector store should back the embeddings?

options.label: Chroma (Recommended)
options.description: Simple embedded/persistent vector DB, first-class LangChain integration (langchain-chroma), minimal setup. Standard default for this kind of prototype and well documented if you get asked about it.

options.label: FAISS
options.description: Lower-level, very fast raw similarity search, but no built-in persistence or metadata filtering story — you'd hand-roll more plumbing (id mapping, save/load, filters).

options.label: sqlite-vec
options.description: Keeps everything in a single sqlite file, consistent with your existing checkpoints/sessions stack. Appealing for 'one database' simplicity, but the library/ecosystem is younger and rougher around the edges than Chroma.

content.text:
Here's the map — same pointers style as before, you drive the implementation.

**1. Dependencies to add** (`requirements.txt`):
```
langchain-milvus
pymilvus
milvus-lite
pymupdf
```
`langchain-text-splitters` and `langchain-ollama` you already have transitively/explicitly. You'll also need to `ollama pull nomic-embed-text` (or another embedding-capable model — check `ollama list` for what you already have; embedding models are separate from chat models).

**2. Ingestion script** — new top-level file, e.g. `ingest.py`, run separately from `main.py` (not part of the REPL):

- **Walk + load**: `langchain_community.document_loaders.PyMuPDFLoader(path).load()` — returns one `Document` per page, each with `.page_content` and `.metadata` (`source`, `page`). Fast and handles well-formatted PDFs cleanly; wrap each file's load in `try/except` and log+skip failures rather than crashing the whole 10GB run — you said "most" are well-formatted, so a few will throw.
- **Chunk**: `langchain_text_splitters.RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter(chunk_size=..., chunk_overlap=...).split_documents(docs)` — this preserves the page metadata onto each chunk automatically, which is what makes citations possible later.
- **Incremental/idempotent tracking**: at 10GB you don't want a re-run to re-embed everything. Keep a small manifest (a sqlite table, or even a plain file) keyed by file path + mtime or a content hash, and skip files already ingested. This is worth designing deliberately — it's the kind of "how do you make this resumable/idempotent" question that comes up in FDE interviews directly.
- **Embed + upsert**: `langchain_ollama.OllamaEmbeddings(model="nomic-embed-text")`, then `langchain_milvus.Milvus(embedding_function=embeddings, connection_args={"uri": "./milvus_rag.db"}, collection_name="domain_docs", auto_id=True)`. A `uri` ending in `.db` is what triggers Milvus Lite (embedded, no server) rather than trying to connect over the network. `.add_documents(chunks)` does the embed+insert.

**3. Retrieval tool** — new file `tools/search_docs.py`, same `@tool` pattern as `calculator.py`:

- Connect to the *same* Milvus collection/uri at module load time (not inside the function — you don't want to reopen the store on every call).
- `vectorstore.similarity_search(query, k=5)` (or `similarity_search_with_score` if you want to reason about relevance thresholds later).
- Format results as a string with source file + page per chunk so the model can cite where an answer came from — this also makes it easy for *you* to sanity-check retrieval quality while testing.
- Register it in `tools/tools_registrar.py`'s `TOOLS` list.

**4. System prompt**: worth updating `.env`'s `SYSTEM_PROMPT` to tell the model this tool exists and roughly what domain it covers — otherwise it has no signal to reach for it over answering from its own (untrained-on-this-domain) knowledge.

**Design things worth deliberately deciding, not defaulting on autopilot** (good to have opinions on going into an interview):
- Chunk size/overlap — depends on how dense/technical the domain text is.
- `k` (how many chunks to retrieve) and whether to filter by similarity score.
- What "citation" format the tool returns, since that shapes how verifiable the model's answers are.

Ping me when you've got a first pass — I'll review same as always.

Before starting to design and code, I just confirmed that i have 12gb of data. What are the implications of the size? Is it a lot or not? They aren't all clean PDFs, not all have PDF sections. Few are hand-scanned with text (mostly) reachable. How do we approach embedding these files as opposed to well formatted markdown files?

**Size:** 12GB of PDF bytes is not a lot in absolute terms for a local RAG pipeline — the number that actually matters is extracted *text* volume, and PDF binary is a poor proxy for that. Well-formatted text PDFs compress a lot (a 50MB PDF might yield only a few MB of text), while scanned pages contribute close to zero extractable text per MB until OCR'd. Realistically your extracted corpus is probably in the hundreds of MB to low-single-digit-GB of raw text — chunked, that's likely somewhere in the hundreds of thousands to low millions of chunks. That's well within Milvus Lite's comfort zone (it's rated for roughly up to ~1M vectors before you'd want standalone Milvus), so storage/indexing isn't the constraint. The real cost is **embedding compute time** — generating embeddings locally via Ollama for that many chunks is the thing that'll actually take hours, not the disk footprint — so the incremental/resumable ingestion design we already talked about isn't just nice-to-have, it's load-bearing here.

**Heterogeneous docs (clean PDF vs. no-section PDF vs. scanned):** the heterogeneity lives entirely in the *extraction* stage — once you have clean text, embedding doesn't care where it came from. Practically that means your loader can't be a single `PyMuPDFLoader(path).load()` call anymore; it needs to be a **fallback chain, decided per page, not just per file** (a single scanned document can still have a handful of real-text pages, and a clean PDF can have a scanned appendix):

1. Try fast text extraction (PyMuPDF) first.
2. Run a quality check on the output — e.g. extracted char count per page below some threshold, or a low ratio of recognizable words — to decide whether that page actually got usable text.
3. If it fails the check, fall back to OCR on that page (render to image via PyMuPDF's `get_pixmap()`, feed to `pytesseract`) — this is orders of magnitude slower than text extraction, which is exactly why you want to gate it behind the quality check rather than OCR-ing everything.
4. Tag chunks with how they were produced (`extraction` vs `ocr`) in metadata — OCR text is noisier (misrecognized characters, broken words), and you'll want that traceable when you're later debugging why retrieval returned something garbled.

For the "no clear sections" PDFs, plain `RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter` is your fallback since there's no structure to exploit — it'll occasionally split mid-thought, which is a known quality ceiling, not a bug to chase. Markdown is the odd one out in the best way: no extraction/OCR concerns at all, and it buys you structure-aware chunking via `MarkdownHeaderTextSplitter` (split on headers) instead of blind character windows — meaningfully better chunk boundaries for free. Worth deciding now whether that split-strategy difference is worth branching your ingestion code on file type, or whether you'd rather normalize everything down to the lowest-common-denominator splitter for simplicity — that's a real tradeoff, not an obvious call.
